faqs.q: What is the formula to convert hourly to annual pay?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual income before tax and super. If you work different hours, adjust the weekly figure accordingly. Remember, this assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual pay calculation?
faqs.a: Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate under most awards. When using our timesheet tool, you can check a box to add the 25% casual loading. Do not enter a rate that already includes loading – the tool adds it for you. For example, if the base rate is $26.44 (National Minimum Wage), casual loading brings it to $33.05 per hour. Your annual pay would then be $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80, plus super on top.

faqs.q: Can you salary sacrifice childcare fees from your gross pay?
faqs.a: Yes, many employers offer salary sacrifice arrangements for childcare fees under a salary packaging plan. This reduces your taxable income, but it does not affect the super guarantee, which is calculated on your ordinary earnings (before sacrifice). The Australian Taxation Office sets rules for fringe benefits tax (FBT) on salary-sacrificed childcare. Check with your employer or a tax professional to see if your workplace offers this option and how it interacts with your hourly-to-annual conversion.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Hourly to Annual Pay

If you earn an hourly wage or have received a salary offer, converting between the two helps you compare jobs and plan your budget. The standard formula in Australia is straightforward: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. This article explains the calculation, the role of awards and the National Minimum Wage, casual loading, superannuation, tax, and how salary sacrifice – including for childcare fees – fits in.

### The Basic Formula

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × weekly hours × 52.

If you work 38 hours per week: annual = hourly × 38 × 52.

For example, on the [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) of $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026):
- Weekly: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80
- Annual: $1,004.90 × 52 = $52,254.80

This is your gross pay before tax and super. The fortnightly figure is useful if you are paid every two weeks – simply double your weekly amount.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage, set by the Fair Work Commission, is the base rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement. However, most workers are covered by a modern award that specifies higher minimum rates for their industry or role. Award rates often include classifications for skill level, experience, and shift work. Always check your [pay guides](/blog) or [reference tables](/data) to confirm the correct rate for your job. The figures here are averages or minimums, not a median for your specific position.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. When using our [timesheet](/), you enter the base rate and tick the casual loading box – do not enter a rate that already includes loading. For the National Minimum Wage, casual loading gives $33.05 per hour. Your annual pay as a casual would be $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80. Note that casual loading is paid on top of the base rate, not instead of it.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Employers must pay the super guarantee at 12% of your ordinary earnings (from 1 July 2026). Super is paid **on top** of your gross pay, not deducted from it. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year – earnings above that do not attract compulsory super. For the minimum wage example:
- Annual super: $52,254.80 × 12% = $6,270.58
- Total cost to employer: $58,525.38

If you salary sacrifice part of your pay (e.g., for childcare fees), super is still calculated on your ordinary earnings before the sacrifice. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your annual gross pay is taxed using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:
- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% for each dollar over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% for each dollar over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% for each dollar over $135,000
- Over $190,000: 45% for each dollar over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (using 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). For a minimum wage earner ($52,254.80):
- Tax: ($45,000 – $18,200) × 15% + ($52,254.80 – $45,000) × 30% = $4,020 + $2,176.44 = $6,196.44
- Medicare: $52,254.80 × 2% = $1,045.10
- Total deductions: $7,241.54
- Take-home: $45,013.26 per year (before any salary sacrifice).

Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a detailed estimate. Remember, this does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging adjustments.

### Can You Salary Sacrifice Childcare Fees?

Yes, many employers offer salary sacrifice arrangements for childcare fees as part of a salary packaging plan. This means you agree to reduce your gross salary in exchange for the employer paying your childcare costs directly. The sacrificed amount is not subject to income tax, which can lower your taxable income. However, it does not reduce your super guarantee – super is still calculated on your ordinary earnings before the sacrifice. The Australian Taxation Office applies fringe benefits tax (FBT) to some salary-sacrificed benefits, but childcare provided through an approved centre may be exempt from FBT up to certain limits. Check with your employer or a tax professional to see if your workplace offers this and how it affects your overall pay. For more on salary packaging, see [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Important Assumptions and Limitations

This conversion assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For a personalised calculation, use our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool or check [average pay](/topics/average-pay) data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The ABS Average Weekly Earnings (May 2026) for full-time adult ordinary time is $2,083.70 per week, which gives an annual equivalent of $108,352.40 (before tax). All employees total earnings average $1,579.20 per week (including part-time workers). These are averages, not medians for your specific job.

### Fortnightly Pay

If you are paid fortnightly, simply multiply your weekly gross by 2. For the minimum wage example: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight. This is helpful for budgeting and comparing with salary offers that are quoted fortnightly.

### Final Thoughts

Understanding your hourly-to-annual conversion helps you evaluate job offers, negotiate pay, and plan your finances. Remember that the National Minimum Wage is a floor – most employees are entitled to higher award rates. Casual loading adds 25% on top. Super is extra. And yes, you can salary sacrifice childcare fees in many workplaces, which may reduce your tax but not your super. Always consult official sources like the Fair Work Ombudsman, Australian Taxation Office, and your employer for your specific situation.
